intro: Hinduism does not have one single holy book. It has a whole library. Some texts are hymns. Some are long stories. Some are talks between a teacher and a student.

In this unit you will learn how Hindus sort these texts. You will learn about shruti, "what is heard," and smriti, "what is remembered." You will also learn how the texts traveled for thousands of years, first by memory and later on palm leaves, in comics and on screens.
By the end, you will be able to name the main Hindu texts. You will be able to say which group each belongs to. You will be able to explain how people kept them alive.
bigQuestion: How have Hindus kept a great library of sacred texts alive for thousands of years?

title: What the Hindu Texts Are

chapters.title: Heard and Remembered: Shruti and Smriti
chapters.bigQuestion: How do Hindus sort their many sacred texts?

story.title: Two Kinds of Words
story.kicker: A grandmother tells her grandson that some words were heard and some were remembered.
paragraphs: Rohan sits beside his grandmother in their apartment in Naperville. A shelf by the window holds many books. Some are thick. Some are thin. Some have gold letters on the cover.
"Which one is the Hindu Bible?" Rohan asks. He heard a friend at school ask that. Grandma laughs softly. "There is no single book," she says. "There is a whole library."

She picks up a thin book of hymns. "Hindus say some words were heard," she says. "Wise seers heard them long, long ago. We call these shruti." Grandma turns the pages gently, as if they were very old.
Then she picks up a big, bright Ramayana. "And some words were remembered," she says. "People remembered them and told them again. These are called smriti."
Rohan looks at the shelf again. Now he sees two groups. Heard and remembered. He wants to know what is in each one. He asks his grandma to tell him more, one group at a time.
story.think: Why might a religion have a whole library instead of one book?

lessons.title: Many Books, Many Voices
lessons.mainIdea: Hinduism has no single holy book but a large library of sacred texts.
reading: Some religions have one main holy book. Hinduism is different. It has a large library of sacred texts. They were made over more than 3,000 years. The oldest texts are older than any city in America.
The library holds hymns, songs, poems and long stories. It also holds teachings and rules for living. Different texts came from different times and places in India.
Hindus sort these texts into two big groups. One group is *shruti*. The other group is *smriti*. In this chapter you will learn what goes in each group.

words.d: holy; treated with deep respect
"what is heard"; the Vedas and Upanishads
"what is remembered"; the epics, Puranas and other texts

lessons.title: The Names Hindu and Sanatana Dharma
lessons.mainIdea: Many Hindus call their tradition Sanatana Dharma, the eternal way.
reading: The word Hindu is old. It comes from the name of the Indus River. People from outside India used it for the people who lived near that river. Today about a billion people call themselves Hindu.
Over time, the word came to mean the religion too. Many Hindus also use another name. They call their tradition *Sanatana Dharma*. That means "the eternal way."
Eternal means lasting forever. Hindus who use this name believe their way has no beginning. Scholars study how the tradition grew and changed over time.

lasting forever, with no beginning or end

lessons.title: Different Favorites
lessons.mainIdea: Different Hindus treasure different texts.
reading: Not every Hindu reads every text. That would take many lifetimes! Different families and groups treasure different books. Many read only a few texts closely and know others through stories.
Some families read the Bhagavad Gita every day. Some love the Ramayana most. Some sing hymns to Shiva or to the Goddess. Many groups follow a teacher who explains certain texts.
There are many groups within Hinduism. Vaishnavas honor Vishnu most. Shaivas honor Shiva. Shaktas honor the Goddess, Devi. Each group has favorite texts.

lessons.title: Seers Who Heard
lessons.mainIdea: Hindus hold that the shruti texts were heard by ancient seers called rishis.
reading: Shruti means "what is heard." Hindus hold that these texts were not made up by people. They believe ancient seers heard them. These seers are called *rishis*.

Many Hindus believe the rishis heard these words in deep meditation. Then they taught them to students. The students taught their own students. Hindus call this long chain of teachers a living tradition.
For this reason, many Hindus treat shruti as the most sacred group of texts. Scholars date the oldest shruti text, the Rig Veda, to about 1500 to 1200 BCE.

words.d: a seer; one of the ancient sages who, Hindus hold, heard the Vedas
sitting quietly and focusing the mind

look.title: Two Ways to Date a Text
look.text: Many Hindus say the Vedas are eternal. They say the rishis heard words that always existed. Scholars look at the language and history. They date the oldest Veda to about 1500 to 1200 BCE. Both views are held today.
look.prompt: How is a traditional view different from a scholar's date?

lessons.title: The Four Vedas
lessons.mainIdea: There are four Vedas, and the Rig Veda is the oldest.
reading: *Veda* means "knowledge." There are four Vedas. They are the Rig Veda, the Sama Veda, the Yajur Veda and the Atharva Veda. All four were first passed on by memory.
The Rig Veda is a book of hymns. A hymn is a song of praise. Many hymns praise Agni, god of fire, and Indra, god of storms. The Sama Veda sets many hymns to melodies.
The Yajur Veda has words for rituals. The Atharva Veda has prayers for health and daily life. Priests still chant verses from the Vedas today at weddings and other rites.

words.d: "knowledge"; one of the four oldest Hindu sacred texts
a song of praise

check.q: What does Veda mean?

lessons.title: The Upanishads
lessons.mainIdea: The Upanishads are shruti texts that ask big questions about the self and the world.
reading: The *Upanishads* come at the end of the Vedas. Many are written as talks between a teacher and a student. They ask big questions. Who am I? What is real?
The Upanishads teach about *Brahman*. Many Hindus understand Brahman as the one reality behind everything. They also teach about *atman*, the true self inside each being.
Scholars date the oldest Upanishads to about 800 to 500 BCE. There are more than 200 texts called Upanishads. About a dozen are the oldest and most famous.

words.d: a shruti text of teachings, often a talk between teacher and student
in the Upanishads, the one reality behind everything

lessons.title: Texts People Remember and Retell
lessons.mainIdea: Smriti texts were remembered and passed on by people, and many Hindus know them best.
reading: Smriti means "what is remembered." Hindus hold that people made these texts. People remembered them and passed them on. They still count as sacred. Many Hindus treat them with great respect all the same.
Smriti includes the two great epics. It includes the Puranas, books of old stories. It includes law books too. Many of the stories children love come from these books.
Shruti is ranked highest. But many Hindus know smriti best. Children grow up hearing the epics. Families act them out at festivals. A child may know the Ramayana long before hearing a Veda.

words.d: a very long poem about heroes and great deeds
a book of old stories about gods, goddesses, kings and the world

lessons.title: The Two Great Epics
lessons.mainIdea: The Ramayana and the Mahabharata are the two great Hindu epics.
reading: Hindus have two great epics. The *Ramayana* tells the story of Rama and Sita. Tradition says the poet Valmiki made it. Rama is honored by many Hindus as an avatar of Vishnu.
The *Mahabharata* tells of a great family and a great war. Tradition says the sage Vyasa made it. It is one of the longest poems in the world. Its story is full of hard choices about what is right.
Scholars think both epics grew over many centuries. They date them roughly between 400 BCE and 400 CE. Hindus have retold them ever since. The stories are still told on stage, on screen and at home.

words.d: the epic of Rama and Sita, credited to Valmiki
the epic of a great family and war, credited to Vyasa

lessons.title: The Gita Inside the Epic
lessons.mainIdea: The Bhagavad Gita is a short, much-loved text inside the Mahabharata.
reading: Inside the Mahabharata is a short text. It is called the *Bhagavad Gita*. The name means "song of the Lord." It has 18 chapters and 700 verses. Most Hindus simply call it the Gita.
In the Gita, the warrior Arjuna does not want to fight. Krishna, his charioteer, teaches him. Many Hindus honor Krishna as God. Their talk takes place on a battlefield, just before a war.
The Gita is smriti. But many Hindus love it as much as any text. Some read a chapter every day. Some learn it by heart. Mahatma Gandhi called the Gita a guide for his whole life.

words.d: "song of the Lord"; Krishna's teaching to Arjuna inside the Mahabharata
the warrior prince whom Krishna teaches in the Bhagavad Gita

lessons.title: Puranas and Law Books
lessons.mainIdea: The Puranas tell stories of the gods, and the law books give rules for living.
reading: There are 18 great Puranas, by traditional count. They tell stories of Vishnu, Shiva, the Goddess and many others. Many stories you know come from them.
The story of Krishna lifting the hill is in the Bhagavata Purana. The story of Prahlada is there too. Families read these stories aloud at festivals and at home.

Smriti also has law books, called Dharma Shastras. They give rules for daily life. People have argued about some of these rules for a long time. Today most Hindus do not follow the old law books word for word.

words.d: a law book giving rules for living
a Purana full of stories of Vishnu and Krishna

chapters.title: Sanskrit, Gurus and Memory
chapters.bigQuestion: How did the Hindu texts travel across thousands of years?

story.title: Forward and Backward
story.kicker: A boy repeats a line forward and backward until he knows every sound by heart.
paragraphs: It is early morning in a school in South India. Ten boys sit cross-legged on a stone floor. Their teacher sits in front of them. He chants a line from the Vedas.

The boys chant it back. Then the teacher chants the line again. This time he chants the words in pairs. One and two. Two and three. Three and four. The room fills with the sound of steady, careful voices.
Next he chants the words backward and forward in a pattern. The boys follow. One boy, Hari, frowns. The pattern is hard. He tries again. He listens closely and moves his lips without a sound.
The teacher waits. Hari tries a third time. This time every sound is right. The teacher nods. Hari smiles. The other boys clap their hands softly for him. Then they all begin the next line together.
Hari's teacher learned the same way from his own teacher. Hindus say this chain goes back thousands of years. Every sound was passed on by memory. Hari hopes to teach it himself one day.
story.think: Why would a teacher make students chant the words in so many patterns?

lessons.title: Sanskrit
lessons.mainIdea: Most of the old Hindu texts are in Sanskrit, an ancient language of India.
reading: Most of the old Hindu texts are in *Sanskrit*. Sanskrit is a very old language of India. The Vedas use an early form of it. Sanskrit has its own careful rules of grammar.
The name Sanskrit means "well made" or "polished." For centuries, scholars and priests used it. Few people speak it at home today. But priests still chant it every day.
Sanskrit is related to many other languages. It is a cousin of Latin, Greek and even English. That is why some Sanskrit words look a little like English words.

words.d: the ancient language of most early Hindu texts
the words and rules people use to speak and write

look.title: Word Cousins
look.text: The Sanskrit word for mother is matr. The Latin word is mater. The Sanskrit word for three is tri. In English it is three. Words that look alike can come from the same very old family.
look.prompt: Why do you think these words look so alike?

check.q: What language are most old Hindu texts in?
check.why: Most early Hindu texts are in Sanskrit.

check.q: What does Sanskrit mean?
check.why: Sanskrit means "well made" or "polished."

check.q: Which language is a cousin of Sanskrit?
check.why: Sanskrit belongs to the same large family as Latin, Greek and English.

lessons.title: Words We Borrowed
lessons.mainIdea: English has borrowed many words from Sanskrit.
reading: You may already know some Sanskrit words. English borrowed them. Guru is one. Karma, yoga and mantra are others. You may hear them in a yoga class or a video game.
Avatar is another borrowed word. In Hindu texts, an *avatar* is a form in which a deity comes into the world. Many Hindus honor Rama and Krishna as avatars of Vishnu.
In English, these words often change meaning. A video game avatar is a picture of you. The Sanskrit word has a much deeper meaning. So it helps to ask what a word means in the old texts.

words.d: a form in which, Hindus believe, a deity comes into the world
a sacred word or phrase that is chanted or repeated

lessons.title: Many Scripts
lessons.mainIdea: Sanskrit can be written in many scripts, and today it is often written in Devanagari.
reading: A script is a set of letters. English uses the Latin alphabet. Sanskrit has been written in many scripts over time. Some scripts use lines and curves. Some use loops and dots.
Today Sanskrit is most often written in *Devanagari*. Hindi uses this script too. Each letter hangs from a line across the top. You can see it on signs and books all across North India.
Long ago, people in different regions wrote Sanskrit in their own local scripts. The sounds stayed the same. Only the letters looked different. A text could travel far and still sound the same.

words.d: a set of letters used to write a language
the script most often used for Sanskrit and Hindi today

lessons.title: Before Writing
lessons.mainIdea: The Vedas were passed down by memory for many centuries before they were written.
reading: The Vedas are very old. For many centuries, nobody wrote them down. Teachers taught them by heart. Students learned every word by listening. They repeated the lines many times each day.
Many Hindus treat the sound of the Vedas as sacred. The exact sounds matter. So it was important not to change even one syllable. A small slip could change the meaning or the sound.

Scholars think the Vedas were written down much later, perhaps in the first thousand years CE. Even then, many teachers kept teaching them by memory. Some families still pass on the chanting this way today.

words.d: spoken or passed on by mouth, not written
one beat of sound in a word

look.title: The Telephone Game
look.text: In the telephone game, a message is whispered down a line. By the end, it often changes. The Vedic teachers had a problem. How could they pass on words for centuries without a single change?
look.prompt: What could you do to keep a message from changing?

check.q: How were the Vedas passed down at first?
check.why: The Vedas were passed down orally, by memory.

check.q: Why did the exact sounds matter?
choices: Many Hindus treat the sound as sacred
check.why: Many Hindus hold the sound of the Vedas to be sacred.

check.q: What does oral mean?
check.why: Oral means spoken, not written.

lessons.title: Chanting Patterns
lessons.mainIdea: Special chanting patterns helped keep every sound the same.
reading: Vedic teachers made clever methods. Students chanted the words straight through. Then they chanted them one at a time. Each way of chanting made them listen very closely.
Next they chanted in pairs: one-two, two-three, three-four. Harder patterns went forward and backward. These patterns have names like krama and ghana.
If a student made a mistake, the patterns showed it. This worked like a checking system. Many scholars say it kept the Rig Veda very close to its old form.

words.d: to sing or speak words in a steady, repeated way
a set order that repeats

look.title: Try a Pattern
look.text: Take four words: red, blue, green, gold. Straight: red blue green gold. In pairs: red blue, blue green, green gold. Now back and forth: red blue, blue red, red blue.
look.prompt: How would these patterns help you catch a mistake?

check.q: What did the chanting patterns help do?
check.why: The patterns worked like a checking system.

check.q: Which is a name of a Vedic chanting pattern?

check.q: What does chant mean?

check.why: To chant is to sing or say words steadily and repeatedly.

lessons.title: A World Treasure
lessons.mainIdea: UNESCO honored Vedic chanting as world heritage in 2003.
reading: UNESCO is part of the United Nations. It honors treasures that belong to all people. Some are buildings. Some are traditions. Places and traditions from all over the world are on its lists.
In 2003, UNESCO named Vedic chanting a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity. Intangible means you cannot touch it. The chanting was written onto UNESCO's official list in 2008.
A song or a chant cannot be touched. But it can be lost if no one learns it. UNESCO hoped to help keep this tradition alive. Schools that teach Vedic chanting still exist in India today.

words.d: the part of the United Nations that honors world heritage
not something you can touch

look.title: Can You Touch a Song?
look.text: Think of a building like the Taj Mahal. You can touch its walls. Now think of a chant your grandparent taught you. You cannot touch it. It lives only while people remember it and pass it on.
look.prompt: How can people protect a treasure that cannot be touched?

check.q: What did UNESCO honor in 2003?
check.why: UNESCO honored Vedic chanting in 2003.

check.q: What does intangible mean?
check.why: Intangible means you cannot touch it.

check.q: Why can a chant be lost?
check.why: An oral tradition lives only if people keep learning it.

lessons.title: Guru and Student
lessons.mainIdea: Hindu texts were passed on from guru to student.
reading: A *guru* is a teacher. In old India, students often lived with their guru. They helped with daily work. They learned texts by heart. Learning could take many years.
The Upanishads often show a guru and a student talking. The student asks a question. The guru answers with a story or an example. This way of learning is still used in many Hindu schools.
Many Hindus still honor their gurus. They see learning as a chain. Each teacher passes on what an earlier teacher gave. Some families invite a guru to bless a child's first lessons.

words.d: a teacher, especially of sacred learning
the most basic, true part of something

look.title: The Salt in the Water
look.text: A father tells his son to put salt in water overnight. In the morning, the son cannot find the salt. But every sip tastes salty. The father says the true self is like that: hidden, yet everywhere.
look.cite: Chandogya Upanishad 6.13, retold from Max Müller's translation, Sacred Books of the East 1 (1879)
look.prompt: How does the salt help the student understand?

check.q: What is a guru?
check.why: A guru is a teacher.

check.q: In old India, where did students often live?
check.why: Students often lived with their guru.

check.q: In the salt lesson, what is the salt compared to?
choices: The true self, hidden but everywhere
check.why: In Chandogya Upanishad 6.13, the salt stands for the hidden true self.

lessons.title: Palm-Leaf Books
lessons.mainIdea: Many texts were later written on dried palm leaves.
reading: Later, people wrote texts down. In much of India, they wrote on dried palm leaves. Each leaf was long and thin. Leaves were easy to find in warm, green parts of India.
Scribes scratched letters into the leaf with a pointed tool. Then they rubbed ink or soot on it. The letters turned dark. This made the writing easy to read and hard to wipe away.
The leaves were tied together with a string. Palm leaves wear out over time. So scribes copied texts again and again. Wooden boards on the top and bottom kept the leaves flat.

words.d: a book or text written by hand
a person who copies texts by hand

look.title: A Bundle of Leaves
look.text: Look at a palm-leaf manuscript in a museum. The leaves are long and narrow, like rulers. Tiny dark letters fill each one. Two wooden boards hold the bundle. A string runs through a hole in the middle.
look.prompt: Why would scribes need to copy these books again and again?

check.q: What did many scribes in India write on?
check.why: Many texts were written on palm leaves.

check.q: What is a manuscript?
check.why: A manuscript is written by hand.

check.q: Why did scribes copy the texts again and again?
check.why: Palm leaves wear out, so texts had to be copied.

lessons.title: Retold in Many Languages
lessons.mainIdea: The stories were retold in Tamil, Hindi and many other languages.
reading: Most people in India did not speak Sanskrit. So poets retold the stories in their own languages. They spoke Tamil, Hindi, Bengali, Marathi and many other languages.
The poet Kamban retold the Ramayana in Tamil, perhaps in the 1100s. The poet Tulsidas retold it in Hindi in the 1500s. His Ramcharitmanas is loved across North India.
The stories spread to many other languages too. Each retelling is a little different. Each helped more people know the stories. Some tell parts of the story that Valmiki's poem does not.

words.d: a story told again in a new way
Tulsidas's Hindi retelling of the Ramayana

check.q: Who retold the Ramayana in Tamil?
check.why: Kamban retold the Ramayana in Tamil.

lessons.title: Comics, TV and Apps
lessons.mainIdea: Today the texts travel through comic books, TV and apps too.
reading: The stories keep traveling. In 1967, Amar Chitra Katha began making comic books of the stories. Many children grew up reading them. The comics used bright pictures and simple words.
In 1987, a TV series of the Ramayana aired in India. Many people stopped what they were doing to watch each Sunday. Streets in many towns became quiet while the show was on.
Today there are cartoons, podcasts and apps. Families in Illinois can read the Gita on a phone. The ways change. The stories keep being told. Temples in Illinois hold classes on the texts as well.

words.d: a show told in many parts
an Indian comic book series that retells old stories, begun in 1967

look.title: Old Story, New Screen
look.text: A girl in Schaumburg opens an app on her tablet. It shows a verse of the Gita in Sanskrit. Under it is the verse in English. She taps a button and hears it chanted.
look.prompt: How is this like the old way of learning? How is it different?

check.why: Amar Chitra Katha made comic books starting in 1967.

check.q: When did the Ramayana TV series air in India?
check.why: The Ramayana TV series began in 1987.

check.q: What stays the same as the ways of telling change?
check.why: New tools carry the same old stories.
